doc.title: Eddie Alley interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

chapter: Metropolitan Life and the Alley band
title: Menlo Park surprise and one of the first black bands in the big hotels
summary: A woman booked him sight unseen, the older crowd loved the band, and he led one of the first black bands in the Fairmont and other big hotels, at union scale.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I’ll never forget one time a woman called me up down around Menlo Park or someplace. She called me up on the telephone and I think I was recommended by somebody, and when I appeared down there and knocked on the door she said to me, “You Eddie Alley?” I said yes. She didn’t know I was black kid you know. I thought she was going to die. I saw all these guys with gray hair and tuxedos and things on, and see that was my thing. I could play beautiful ballads and things, you know, “Fascination” and all those kinds of stuff. I had that kind of a band. I didn’t play boom-bam-boom-bam-boom or — I played where they could dance together. I sized the people up in about four or five tunes. “Where’d you get this band, this is the best band you ever had.” And before I left, “Mr. Alley you’ve got this date, Mr. Alley you’ve got this date.”
That’s cool. Well that’s a big part of being a successful musician is reading the crowd, right?

Yes. That was the first black bands that ever played at any of the hotels. the Fairmont, the Mount Hopkins, all the big hotels, I was one of the first black bands that ever played any of these hotels.
Yeah. What kind of money would your band have played for?
Well whatever the union was in those days, scale, union scale. I forgot what it was. I forgot what the scale was in those days. It was all right. I should have brought my sales book but I didn’t.
